definition.text: A market problem in which one side of a deal knows something the other does not, and uses that hidden information to get a better bargain.

facts.text: The less-informed side may protect itself by pulling out, demanding different prices or staying away, which shrinks trade and competition.
George Akerlof's 1970 paper 'The Market for Lemons' showed how hidden flaws in used cars can make such a market collapse.
It was first described for life insurance: if smokers pay the same premium as non-smokers, smokers buy more cover, raising the insurer's claims.
In contract theory, adverse selection means the agent holds private information before the contract is signed; moral hazard arises after.
Remedies include reputation systems such as eBay's ratings, screening by the uninformed side, warranties and lemon laws.
Voluntary green labelling of bonds is seen as open to greenwashing and adverse selection because of weak oversight.
Fixing one problem can worsen another: mandatory insurance against adverse selection may add to moral hazard.
In health insurance, healthy people may skip cover while those with existing conditions buy it, pushing premiums up for everyone left.

definition.text: A property of a mechanism or set of rules under which every participant does best for themselves by reporting their true preferences.

facts.text: Example: if an insurer sells discounted cover only to high-risk clients, the scheme is incentive-compatible when high-risk clients gain by admitting their risk and low-risk clients lose by pretending.
The concept is credited to the economist Leonid Hurwicz.
In the strong form, truth-telling is best whatever others do, as in a second-price auction; in the weaker form, it is best if everyone else is truthful.
Lindahl taxes based on surveys are not incentive-compatible, because people gain by misreporting how much they value a public good.

definition.text: The result that any outcome that can be achieved by some strategic mechanism can also be achieved by an incentive-compatible one, in which everyone simply tells the truth.

facts.text: It comes in two versions, matching the dominant-strategy and Bayesian–Nash forms of incentive compatibility.
It means a mechanism designer need only consider games in which people truthfully report their private information.

definition.text: A situation in which someone has a reason to take more risk because they will not bear the full cost if things go wrong.

facts.text: An insured firm may take on more risk knowing its insurer will pay; someone with theft insurance may be less careful about locking their car.
It arises from hidden actions after a deal is made, while adverse selection comes from hidden information before it.
The term goes back to the 17th century in insurance; from the 1960s, starting with Ken Arrow, economists used it without any suggestion of fraud.
If health care costs $10 a unit and demand is Q = 20 − P, a person buys 10 units; with free insurance they use 20, and the insurer pays.
Bailouts can encourage future risky lending if lenders believe they will not carry the full losses.
Many argue moral hazard helped cause the 2008 financial crisis, through fund managers, mortgage originators and banks seen as 'too big to fail'.
Firms reduce it with performance-based pay, monitoring and screening.

definition.text: The clash of interests that arises when one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and may pursue its own goals instead.

facts.text: Familiar pairs are managers and shareholders, elected officials and citizens, and brokers and the buyers and sellers they serve.
The problem worsens the more the two sides' interests and information differ and the less the principal can punish the agent.
The losses from an agent straying from the principal's interest are called agency costs.
Principal–agent models study either moral hazard, from hidden actions, or adverse selection, from hidden information.
The theory emerged in the 1970s from economics and institutional theory.
Contracts try to tie pay to performance through piece rates, share options, bonuses, promotions and profit sharing; switching from salary to piece rates raised productivity by 44% in one study.
Jaffe and Stavins in 1994 described the landlord–tenant problem as a principal–agent barrier to adopting cost-effective energy efficiency.
Common property regimes can avoid the principal–agent problem, one reason their local knowledge often beats rules designed by outside experts.

definition.text: A sealed-bid auction for a single item in which the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid.

facts.text: It is a special case of the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism, and losers pay nothing.
Second-price auctions are a typical example of mechanisms where telling the truth is a dominant strategy.

definition.text: A branch of economics and game theory that designs rules, called mechanisms, so that good outcomes result even when the designer cannot see people's true preferences or information.

facts.text: It works backwards from a desired result to a game that produces it, so it is sometimes called reverse game theory.
Example: a buyer wants to know a used car's true quality but cannot just ask, since the seller gains by lying; the buyer can instead set rules that shape the seller's behaviour.
Each player has private information, called its type, and may misreport it; the designer commits to rules that turn reports into an allocation of goods and money transfers.
Thanks to the revelation principle, the designer need only consider mechanisms in which people truthfully report their private information.
Uses include market design, voting theory, internet routing, e-commerce and the advertising auctions of Facebook and Google.
Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson won the 2007 Nobel prize for founding the theory; William Vickrey's related work earned the 1996 prize.

definition.text: Vickrey's 1961 result that, under certain conditions, a large class of auctions all give the seller the same expected revenue, the best the seller can get.

facts.text: It needs buyers with independent types from a continuous distribution and an auction that sells to the buyer who values the good most.
To earn more, a seller must risk giving the item to a lower-valuing buyer, which usually means risking not selling it at all.

definition.text: An impossibility result showing that, with three or more options, any rule that makes truthful reporting always worthwhile must be dictatorial.

facts.text: A rule is dictatorial when one person always gets their most-favoured outcome.
Mechanism design can be seen as a search for ways around it, by changing the model to allow a wider range of mechanisms.

definition.text: The 1983 result that two parties who each privately know how much a good is worth to them cannot always trade it efficiently without risking a loss for one side.

facts.text: It is among the most striking negative results in economics, a kind of mirror image of the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.

definition.text: The study of how people and firms design agreements with each other, usually when one side knows more than the other.

facts.text: Its classic problems are moral hazard, adverse selection and signalling, and it looks for ways to motivate agents to act well.
A leading application is designing the best pay schemes for managers.
It began with Ronald Coase's 1937 article 'The Nature of the Firm'; Kenneth Arrow gave the first formal economic treatment in the 1960s.
Complete contract theory treats firms and markets alike as contracts in which both sides foresee every future situation; it is equivalent to principal–agent theory.
Oliver Hart and Bengt Holmström won the 2016 Nobel prize for it: Holmström on incentives and risk, Hart on gaps in contracts left by an unpredictable future.
Its models usually treat people as maximizing expected utility and solve for the best decisions mathematically.

definition.text: Contracts that cannot spell out what happens in every possible situation, because writing a complete one would be too hard or too costly.

facts.text: A complete contract would set the legal consequences of every possible state of the world.
Oliver Hart and coauthors pioneered the theory, which studies how this inability affects incentives, for example for relationship-specific investments.
A leading application is the Grossman–Hart–Moore property rights theory of the firm.
The law supplies default rules to fill the gaps that parties leave.

title: Absolute and relative performance pay
article: Contract theory#Rewards on Absolute Performance and Relative Performance

definition.text: Two ways to reward workers: in proportion to what each achieves (absolute) or by ranking workers against each other (relative).

facts.text: Absolute performance pay is widely used, but it invites cheating and is exposed to recessions or sudden growth.
Rewarding a whole group for its performance lets some members slack while others work hard.

definition.text: The basic contract-theory model in which a principal who cannot observe an agent's effort chooses a pay scheme tied to output to maximize expected profit.

facts.text: Pay must satisfy a participation constraint, so the agent accepts the deal, and an incentive-compatibility constraint, so the agent prefers the intended effort.
Pay tied to observable output gives the agent incentives to act in the principal's interest.
With a risk-averse agent such contracts are only second-best, because strong incentives rule out full insurance.

title: Job-market signalling

definition.text: Michael Spence's model in which job seekers show employers their hidden ability by earning education credentials.

facts.text: Employers cannot observe a candidate's ability, so there is an information gap that credentials can narrow.
Signals are credible when they cost low-quality senders more to produce or imitate than high-quality ones.
Spence's key assumption is that able workers pay less, in effort, time and stress as well as money, for each unit of education.
Spence found education can be valuable as a signal even if it adds nothing to a worker's productivity.
Many equilibria are possible, and without signalling everyone would be paid the average product, so low-ability workers lose when signalling exists.
The 'sheepskin effect' is the wage gain from holding a diploma beyond the return to the extra year of study, seen when comparing drop-outs and completers.
Studies find signalling a statistically significant influence on wages, alongside factors such as age, sex and geography.

notes: Signalling (economics)#Job-market signalling contains editors' 'Edit: note that this is incorrect...' sentences (S:6197f63c2320, S:94c23f2b9ac0, S:c2a599e0b3e4); not cited.

definition.text: The use of brand reputation by firms to signal quality and reliability to buyers who cannot judge them directly.

facts.text: A study found that information websites raised visits to unbranded sellers and cut visits to branded ones, suggesting better information weakens brand spending.
Certifications and third-party endorsements can add credibility to brand claims.

definition.text: Insurers' efforts to find out how risky each customer is, and so how likely a claim is, before offering cover.

facts.text: Rothschild and Stiglitz showed how an uninformed insurer can draw out customers' risk levels by offering incentives to reveal them.
This lets insurers sort customers into risk classes and offer choices such as higher deductibles for lower premiums.
Tools include background checks and demographic data; a young man, for example, is likelier to crash a car than a middle-aged woman.

definition.text: Models in which a principal, facing an agent with private information about its type, offers a menu of contracts designed so different types pick different ones.

facts.text: The best type usually trades as much as it would with full information ('no distortion at the top'), while other types trade less.
Optimal auction design is a many-agent version of the basic screening model; Roger Myerson and Eric Maskin pioneered these models.
Applications include regulation, public procurement and price discrimination, and the models have been tested in laboratory and field data.

definition.text: A situation in which one side of a deal has more or better information than the other.

facts.text: It gives one side more power in a deal and can make trades inefficient, in the worst case causing market failure.
A used-car seller usually knows the car's condition far better than the buyer.
Its main forms are adverse selection, moral hazard and monopolies of knowledge.
It contrasts with perfect information, a key assumption of neoclassical economics.
Firms know better than regulators what they would do without regulation, which can weaken the rules.
Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for analysing markets with asymmetric information.
Distrust between buyers and sellers can lead to opportunistic behaviour and even to a market breaking down.

title: The Market for Lemons

definition.text: George Akerlof's 1970 paper showing how markets behave when buyers cannot judge quality, using the used-car market.

facts.text: In the model the seller knows a car's exact quality, while the buyer only knows the chance it is a bad car, a 'lemon'.
It brought information problems to the forefront of economic theory.
It arises when buyers cannot judge quality before buying, sellers gain by passing off bad goods as good, and sellers have no credible way to prove quality.
A lack of reputation, regulation, guarantees or warranties to assure quality also helps produce it.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether a lemons market actually exists in used vehicles (S:29ec2fbd1b20).

definition.text: A way for the better-informed side to show its type believably to the other side and so reduce an information gap.

facts.text: Michael Spence first proposed it and coined the term.
Spence's example: finishing college can signal an ability to learn to employers.

definition.text: A way for the less-informed side to get the other side to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices.

facts.text: Joseph Stiglitz pioneered the theory of screening.
Signalling and screening both resemble voluntary disclosure of information.

definition.text: Rules that require the better-informed party to reveal information, used when voluntary disclosure does not happen.

facts.text: The US Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Fair Disclosure requires companies to disclose material information to investors.
That rule reduced information asymmetry, as seen in lower trading costs.
